bib.title: DERA: Enhancing Large Language Model Completions with Dialog-Enabled Resolving Agents

read.skipped: Appendix QA example chats (A.1) and the rewrite/care-plan prompt bodies were skimmed, not read line by line.

question: Can two role-scoped GPT-4 agents (a Researcher and a Decider) that converse iteratively improve the accuracy and completeness of GPT-4 outputs on clinical text tasks?
hypothesis: Pairing an information-focused Researcher with a decision-making Decider, working iteratively in dialog, yields higher-quality output than a single prompt or chaining, especially for long-form generation.
contributions: DERA (Sec 2): a framework for agent-agent dialog to improve performance on natural language tasks.
Evaluation on three clinical tasks: medical conversation summarization, care plan generation, open-ended medical QA.
Human-expert and quantitative evidence that DERA beats base GPT-4 on summarization and care plans, with little to no gain on QA.
Release of an open-ended version of MedQA (NEJM set not releasable).

method.summary: Two GPT-4 prompts play Decider and Researcher and converse. The Decider drafts an output, the Researcher points out problems, the Decider accepts or rejects each and writes accepted ones to a shared scratchpad, and a final prompt rewrites the output from draft plus scratchpad. For QA the Decider is seeded with the self-consistency vote distribution and a Researcher that only points to question parts, ending in a 5-sample vote.
method.task: clinical text generation: medical chat summarization, care plan generation, open-ended and multiple-choice medical QA

datasets.name: Telehealth chat encounters (summarization)
datasets.size: 500 encounters; 50-encounter random subset for human evaluation
datasets.split: 500 for quantitative corruption study, 50 for physician study
datasets.source: chat-based telehealth platform (Curai), de-identified; not released
datasets.preprocessing: De-identified and scrubbed of PHI. 27 dialog turns on average (min 9, max 82); 646 unigram tokens on average (min 42, max 2031).

datasets.name: Care plan encounters
datasets.split: same 50 as the summarization human evaluation

datasets.name: MedQA US (open-ended rewrite)
datasets.size: 1178 dev questions (sampled from train), 1273 test questions
datasets.split: dev = sample of training set; test as formulated by the MedQA authors
datasets.source: Jin et al. 2021 (USMLE); open-ended version released at github.com/curai/curai-research
datasets.preprocessing: GPT-4 rewrote the final sentence (Prompt 13) or full question (Prompt 12) to be open-ended, temperature 0; automated, may contain errors; images not excluded.

datasets.name: NEJM continuing-education questions (open-ended rewrite)
datasets.split: split by area; 7 areas (Reproductive, Gastrointestinal, Neurologic/Psychogenic, Special Sensory, Endocrine, Musculoskeletal, Maternity Care) reserved as dev
datasets.source: New England Journal of Medicine; cannot be released for licensing

other.version: GPT-4 as available Feb 2023 for the MCQ and dev-set QA runs; the 'latest version at the time' otherwise; exact snapshot not named
other.roles: same model plays Decider, Researcher, corruptor, metric extractor/verifier and answer-similarity judge

inference.decoding: OpenAI chat API sampling; per-prompt temperature, max tokens, top_p, frequency penalty (Tables 5 and 6)
inference.temperature: Summarization/care plan: 1 for generation prompts, 0 for GPT-F1 extractor and verifier. QA: 0.7 for 1-shot, 0 for Decider initial message, 0.3 for Researcher-Decider turns, 0 for final answer and similarity
inference.max_tokens: Summarization/care plan: 512 (200 for GPT-F1 prompts). QA: 50 (1-shot), 400 (Decider initial msg), 250 (Researcher/Decider turns), 100 (final answer, similarity)
inference.samples: QA baseline: 5 completions of the 1-shot prompt, majority vote (ties: first completion of highest-ranking answers). DERA final: 5 completions with chat history, majority vote. Single run only ('we only report single runs').
inference.prompting: Summarization/care plan: zero-shot role prompts (Prompts 1-11); care plan initial prompt includes an example. QA: 1-shot prompt (Prompt 14); Researcher and Decider prompts act as expert doctors; MCQ variant gives options and asks for letter A-D.
inference.retrieval: None. Researcher uses the encounter text (summarization) or GPT-4 internal knowledge and the question only (QA).

parameters.scratchpad: Decider appends accepted corrections; final prompt applies them to the original output
parameters.qa_decider_init: vote distribution over 5 one-shot answers turned into a 3-4 sentence rationale (Prompt 15)

metrics.name: GPT-F1
metrics.definition: Harmonic mean of GPT-Recall and GPT-Precision. Medical entities extracted (Prompt 6) per summary section from predicted and ground-truth text; a verification prompt (Prompt 7) checks presence incl. rephrasings. Recall = tp_gt/(tp_gt+fn), Precision = tp_pred/(tp_pred+fp). Ground truth is the uncorrupted GPT-4 summary.

metrics.name: Physician preference
metrics.definition: 4 licensed physicians pick Initial or Final summary / care plan per encounter

metrics.name: Information captured
metrics.definition: Physician rating All/Most/Some/None of clinical info (or care steps) captured

metrics.name: GPT-4 Exact
metrics.definition: GPT-4 binary judge whether predicted and gold answers are the same medical concept (Prompt 20)

metrics.name: GPT-4 Sim
metrics.definition: GPT-4 relatedness score 0-1 of predicted vs gold answer (Prompt 19); out-of-range outputs set to 0 unless all are 100

metrics.name: BERTScore F1
metrics.definition: Average BERTScore F1 between gold and generated answers, scibert-basevocab-uncased

eval.protocol: Summarization quantitative: GPT-4 summaries on 500 encounters treated as ground truth, synthetically corrupted, DERA asked to repair. Human study: 4 physicians on 50 encounters, not the treating clinicians for care plans. Single run for QA, no significance tests reported.

availability.data: open-ended MedQA released; NEJM and telehealth chats not released

prompts.text: You (Person A) are a very good summary writer for medical dialogues between physicians and patients. ... You are generally very confident about the summary you wrote, however, when presented with compelling arguments by the verifying summary writer, you add to the correction scratchpad. You also suggest any edits of your own in case you notice a mistake. ... Question: What do you say next? Respond to Person B in the tag [RESPONSE: "<your_response_here>"] and output any corrections to add to the scratchpad in the tag [SCRATCHPAD: "<things_to_add_to_the_scratchpad_here>"].

You (Person B) are a very good summary editer for medical dialogues between physicians and patients. ... Go through each section of the summary one at a time and point out any text that does not have a grounding in the dialogue. It must be possible to directly tie any span of the summary to the dialogue. ... Person A may not initially agree with you, but if you are confident there is an error do your best to convince Person A of the mistake. ... output the tag "[STOP]".
Make all changes mentioned in the scratchpad to the original summary to output the corrected summary. Output the tag "[STOP]" when finished writing the corrected summary.

Using the above dialogue and provided summary, corrupt the summary slightly. This could include moving a positive symptom to be a negative symptom, making up medical history mentioned, etc. ... Note that any changes/corruption should make the summary less factual. Desired Corruption Level: {corruption_level}/10

You are an expert medical doctor who is guiding a medical student through thinking about which of several answers is best for a given question. You cannot give the student the answer. Your role is to help the student think through the question, specifically by pointing out portions of the question that are important in understanding the problem. Rules; - All responses should include a quote from the question. ... - Responses should be at most 4 sentences long.

You are an expert doctor who is trying to select the answer to a medical question, and is willing to be open-minded about their answer. ... You can change your answer at any point, but do not assume that the expert knows the exact answer and is providing leading questions. ... Respond with the option you believe most likely to be the right answer ("Answer:<SHORT ANSWER>") and a response to that message ("Response:<MESSAGE>"):

prompts.purpose: Decider initial message from vote distribution (Prompt 15)

limits: QA shows little to no improvement over GPT-4 self-consistency baseline; authors attribute it to the need for a single granular answer.
Single runs only for QA (cost); no significance tests.
GPT-4 grades itself (GPT-F1, Exact, Sim); authors flag this as problematic.
Corruption study treats GPT-4 summaries as ground truth and the corruptions are synthetic and generated by GPT-4.
Human studies: 50 encounters, 4 physicians, one telehealth population; harmfulness numbers too small to generalise.
Possible MedQA contamination; GPT-4 snapshots not persisted so results hard to reproduce.
Open-ended rewrites are automated with only quality checks; NEJM and telehealth data not released.
Role ablations (single agent vs two, no scratchpad, turn count) are not reported, so the Researcher's contribution is not isolated from simply a second revision pass.

terms.definition: Dialog-Enabled Resolving Agents: a framework for agent-agent dialog to improve output on natural language tasks
agent that reviews information and suggests what is likely crucial; not treated as the source of truth
agent that starts the conversation, responds to the Researcher, and has final authority over the output; never has to defer
shared memory to which the Decider writes accepted corrections, used to produce the final output instead of regenerating each turn

lineage.note: contrasted: CoT performs researcher and decider roles jointly
chaining sub-tasks, which DERA replaces with iterative holistic refinement
